tx.t: In this lecture we will look at the diversity of languages around the world. There are about seven thousand languages spoken today.
About forty per cent of them are endangered, which means they are at risk of disappearing. Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers, while English is the most widely spoken language overall.
Just twenty-three languages account for more than half of the world's population. A language usually disappears when children stop learning it at home.

tx.t: Today I would like to describe a bike-sharing scheme in the town of Ashby. It began in twenty ten with eight hundred and thirty-five bikes, placed at stations around the centre.
Use grew quickly. Within three years the number of journeys had risen by twenty-one per cent, and on a busy day there were more than three thousand trips.
The scheme soon met a serious problem: bikes being left in the wrong places. The council solved it with marked parking zones with a small fine for leaving a bike outside them.
Today, a ride costs two pounds twenty-five for the first half hour, and the first fifteen minutes are free for residents.

tx.t: This lecture is about a successful conservation project in the Calder Estuary. In nineteen eighty-four, only thirty-five pairs of bats were counted there.
The main reason for the decline was disturbance from walkers and dogs. So volunteers and rangers created protected zones with quiet paths.
By twenty nineteen, the number had risen to four hundred and eight pairs, which shows that careful management can work.

tx.t: Today I would like to talk about the Silk Road, one of the greatest trade networks in history. It was not a single road but a network of routes connecting China with the Mediterranean.
The main routes were more than six thousand kilometres long. The Chinese envoy Zhang Qian travelled west around one hundred and thirty BC and helped to open the routes.

Cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara, in what is now Uzbekistan, became rich and famous centres of trade. Besides silk, merchants carried spices, paper, glass and precious stones, and also ideas and religions.
The routes became less important when sea trade grew cheaper in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

tx.t: This lecture is about the short history of the internet. The first network, ARPANET, linked four American research sites in nineteen sixty-nine.

Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist working at CERN, invented the World Wide Web at the end of the nineteen eighties. The web and the internet are not the same thing: the internet is the network, and the web is one service that runs on it.
Google was founded in nineteen ninety-eight by two students at Stanford University. Today, more than five billion people use the internet.

tx.t: This morning we are going to look at some basic facts about the Moon. The Moon is about three hundred and eighty-four thousand kilometres from the Earth.
It takes about twenty-seven days to orbit the Earth once. The same side of the Moon always faces us, because its rotation takes exactly as long as its orbit.
The Moon is about a quarter of the width of the Earth. Gravity on the Moon is only about one-sixth of gravity on Earth.

tx.t: Researchers at Northfield College carried out a study in twenty twenty-one to find out how students prepare for exams. They followed three hundred and twenty-two students over eleven weeks.
On average, the students studied for six hours a day. However, only sixty-nine per cent of them used any planned method.
The students who used the method of testing themselves instead of rereading scored higher in the final exam. The researchers concluded that how you study may matter more than how long you study.
